posts.title: Olivie Blake’s latest is “a gory, gothic masterpiece”
posts.text:
Olivie Blake's latest is "a gory, gothic masterpiece" — Book Pix
By Genevieve, Books Content Manager @ Pix

August is kind of a weird month: summer isn't over, fall hasn't started, and everyone is scrambling to take a few more days of vacation. So why not lean into the weirdness? Today's books are delightfully off-kilter, with a bloody Hollywood tale, some multiverse romance, and more.

FANTASY SPOTLIGHT — Dreamland by Olivie Blake
New York Times bestselling author Olivie Blake (The Atlas Six, Girl Dinner) returns with a bloody good novel about an aspiring actress who is drawn into the orbit of a powerful Hollywood dynasty, as a seductive heir and her own ambition threaten to consume her. Alix E. Harrow (Starling House) raves: "This is Olivie Blake at the height of her power, doing cartwheels on the high wire. Dreamland is a sweat-slick Hollywood fable about fame, fortune, and the sins we'd commit for either. A gory, gothic masterpiece."

ROMANCE SPOTLIGHT — In What World by Bridget Morrissey
In this "true love letter to theatre kids and queer folks" (Hannah Bonam-Young), two former high school rivals begrudgingly reunite to find their missing drama teacher, only to tumble through a series of alternate realities where other versions of themselves are much more honest about their feelings for each other. Equal parts multiverse adventure and simmering second-chance romance, this clever, heartfelt novel asks what happens when the person you can't stand might be the person you can't live without.

THE REVIEWS ARE IN
"A tour de force." —The Atlantic
"A rare and beautifully controlled novel of magic, intrigue, and obsession…. Delightful and dangerous. A feat of marvelous showmanship!" —Rachel Beanland, author of This House Is on Fire
"One of the most unusual, thought-provoking books you'll read this year." —BookPage

BOOKWORLD
Watch the brand-new trailer for Verity. Roxane Gay's Hunger is coming to Lifetime in September. Can you couch-to-5k your way back into reading?

Guess the Book (emoji edition) answer: Dandelion Wine by Ray Bradbury, the ultimate late-summer read.

Hawaii movie marathon — Travel Pix

Aloha! This week, we've got a Hawaiian-set roundup—the movies, shows, and books that capture the best of what the islands have to offer.

ACTOR SPOTLIGHT
Jason Momoa isn't just Hollywood's most famous Native Hawaiian actor—from Aquaman to Chief of War, he's helped bring Hawaiian culture and language to a global audience. Off-screen, he uses that spotlight to give back to the islands, working on beach cleanups and serving as an ocean-advocacy ambassador for the UNEP to help protect the coastlines he calls home.

The Wrecking Crew — streaming on Prime Video. Estranged half-brothers James (Dave Bautista) and Jonny (Jason Momoa) reunite in Hawaii after their father's murder, uncovering a scheme to seize Hawaiian land.

Chief of War — streaming on Apple TV. Momoa stars as Ka'iana, a fearless warrior on a mission to unite Hawaii's warring kingdoms before Western colonizers arrive in this epic drama series about the origin of Hawaii.

ULTIMATE HAWAII MOVIE MARATHON
A viewing list of Hawaii-set films.

ISLAND LIFE: BOOKS MADE FOR BEACH DAYS
True to Me by Kay Bratt — On Maui, matriarch Ava Briscoe runs the family's pineapple farm as her four grown children each navigate life's hurdles. But when a long-buried secret resurfaces, exposing betrayal and threatening the business, the family is forced to face some hard truths.

Also recommended: Soul Surfer, Avatar: The Way of Water, Lilo & Stitch, The Unhoneymooners, Blue Hawaiian, Shark Dialogues.

PAW Patrol takes on bedtime — Family Pix

Ready for a prehistoric family adventure? We put together the ultimate family night this week to make movie night—and bedtime—even more fun. Start with PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie, then keep the excitement going with books perfect for little dinosaur fans.

FAMILY MOVIE NIGHT

The most chilling true crime shows of 2026 — Today's Pix

Earlier this summer, Netflix's Maternal Instinct had everyone talking about its chilling depiction of a real COVID-era case. Now, a new season of Conversations with a Killer is landing this week. With the genre having a killer lineup this summer, we've rounded up the most fascinating true crime stories across TV, podcasts, and books.

THE MOST CHILLING TRUE CRIME SHOWS OF THE YEAR (SO FAR)
True crime TV isn't just popular right now, it's absolutely dominating. These are the new shows that made viewers stay up way past their bedtime, one creepy episode at a time.
Conversations with a Killer: The Charles Manson Tapes — Joe Berlinger's docuseries returns for a new volume, tracing Charles Manson's rise as a cult leader through unreleased prison recordings, firsthand accounts, and archival footage most viewers have never seen. It's the franchise's darkest season yet, and the closest anyone's gotten to hearing Manson explain himself in his own words. Only on Netflix August 12.

NEW & UNSETTLING TRUE CRIME PODCASTS
From mysterious cold cases to shocking family secrets nobody saw coming, the best true crime podcasts of the year prove the genre still has new angles to explore.
The Idiot — For years, M. Gessen wrote about the world's worst people: dictators, terrorists, human rights abusers. Then their own cousin Allen got arrested for trying to have his ex-wife killed. Serial Productions' latest is the studio's funniest true crime podcast yet, and its most personal.

PAGE-TURNERS: THE MOST ADDICTIVE TRUE CRIME BOOKS OF 2026
The best true crime writing turns real tragedy into something you can't put down without ever losing the human stakes.
London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe — Patrick Radden Keefe, the writer behind Say Nothing and Empire of Pain, tells the story of a London teenager who invented an entire identity as a Russian oligarch's son before he was found dead in the Thames. This devastating and spellbinding read is easily one of the biggest books of the year.

posts.title: “A rollicking, hilarious tale of shipwreck, shenanigans and murder”
posts.text:
"A rollicking, hilarious tale of shipwreck, shenanigans and murder" — Book Pix
By Genevieve, Senior Books Content Manager @ Pix

Today's Book Pix is delightfully unhinged. From an NSFW rabbit hole to a shipwreck-fueled family drama, Karin Slaughter's newest page-turner, and a literary classic getting a very modern adaptation, today's picks are guaranteed to keep you on your toes.

IS SENTIENT OBJECT SMUT HAVING A MOMENT?
As my colleagues and I cackled over all the early Wicker memes, I felt the need to point out that sentient object smut is an actual romance subgenre. And just like Wicker, they frequently serve a hefty dose of humor along with their spice.
Unhinged by Vera Valentine — In this paranormal romance, a woman must trust the sentient front door that's secretly protected her for years when a deadly stalker threatens her life. As odd as it may sound, this book has a cult following: more than 10k reviews on Amazon and almost 30k on Goodreads. The door is actually a dryad shifter who gets stuck in door form, so there's a Greek mythology angle. Readers agree it is totally bonkers, yet somehow completely delightful.

THE BIG DEBUT — The Responsible Party by Claire Carusillo
When a modern-day scandal and a decades-old murder collide, a canceled skincare influencer uncovers the wild history of the "unsinkable" women who came before her. Vulture calls this debut about an unforgettable family "pleasurably busy and delightfully odd," while The New York Times hails it as "a rollicking, hilarious tale of shipwreck, shenanigans and murder."

THRILLER SPOTLIGHT — The Secrets We Hide by Karin Slaughter
Sheriff Clifton is back in the next North Falls mystery from #1 New York Times bestselling author Karin Slaughter, the powerhouse behind The Good Daughter and the Will Trent series. Expect buried secrets, mounting suspicions, and plenty of twists as Clifton and her sister unravel what really happened to the Vickery family one terrible night. Freida McFadden: "Few writers can balance pulse-pounding suspense and emotional truth as brilliantly as Karin Slaughter."

PAGE TO SCREEN — My Brilliant Career
A 125-year-old novel is getting a very 2026 glow-up. Premiering August 13 on Netflix, My Brilliant Career gives Miles Franklin's 1901 classic a wildly modern makeover, following aspiring writer Sybylla Melvyn (Philippa Northeast) as she chooses creative ambition over marriage and society's expectations in early 20th-century Australia. Created by an all-female team of writers, producers, and directors.

BOOKWORLD
Barack Obama is launching a podcast about his favorite books. This poet has a powerful idea about what reading can do. Heated Rivalry has cast its Troy and Harris.
Guess the Book answer: Verity by Colleen Hoover — the adaptation starring Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson, and Josh Hartnett is less than two months away.

posts.title: One family. One storm. Six hours.
A millennial’s guide to YA television
Trust the process
posts.text:
Trust the process — Wellness Pix

Today we're celebrating the return of Ted Lasso and the inspiration the show continues to give us. Ted is starting over, trading the men's team for a second-division women's team. Once again, he proves that ability isn't fixed. It's built through effort, curiosity, and a willingness to feel unsure before you feel capable. We're borrowing the Season 4 mantra, "trust the process," to find the confidence and motivation to tackle anything.

TRAILER OF THE DAY — Ted Lasso Season 4
This season, Ted's back in Richmond, but this time he's leading a second division women's football squad instead of the men's team he's known for. Along the way, he and the players discover what it means to take a chance before they've worked out every detail, trusting that they'll figure it out once they land.

STORIES OF REINVENTION & GROWTH
Growth isn't always graceful. These films remind us that real change happens one uncertain step at a time.
Brittany Runs a Marathon — streaming on Prime Video. Brittany, overwhelmed and feeling stuck, decides to run a marathon with zero experience. Through consistent effort and support from unlikely friends, she discovers that real transformation comes from trusting the small steps.

PAIRED READING
Theory and story can be even more powerful together. We're pairing the research behind "growth mindset" with a novel that brings the idea to life.
Mindset by Carol S. Dweck, Ph.D. — Psychologist Carol Dweck reveals why some people give up while others push through. Success is shaped by how we respond to failure and challenges. This research-backed guide shows how embracing effort and curiosity, over perfection, transforms what we're capable of achieving.
The Midnight Library by Matt Haig — Between life and death exists a library holding infinite versions of your life. Nora gets to try them all, discovering that no single choice defines her worth. A moving reminder that growth means embracing uncertainty and curiosity, not chasing one "perfect" path.

Top 3 ultimate beach reads — Insider Pix

Welcome back to Insider Pix, where we uncover what entertainment and culture insiders are watching, reading, and listening to.

A senior marketing executive with more than 16 years of experience across retail, CPG, and technology. She has spent the past seven years as Vice President of Sales and Marketing at ThriftBooks, leading the company's marketing strategy across brand, media, and growth.

A hidden gem you wish more people knew about?
"I am a product of the '80s and love classics from those years, with a special place in my heart for series like The Hardy Boys and Sweet Valley High. They are classic books that I encourage people to go back and reread. You can be assured that AI did not write those books. Plus, it is fun to remember what life was like without internet and cell phones."

Best TV show you've watched recently?
"I'm a big fan of Taylor Sheridan, so I am having my fill with Dutton Ranch and Lioness Season 3. I've also enjoyed some of the newer series this summer like Off Campus, Elle, and thrilling book-to-screen adaptations like I Will Find You."

Best movie you watched recently?
"The Odyssey was spectacular. I studied Latin through college, and my high school Latin teacher also taught us Greek and Roman mythology. I remember reading The Iliad and The Odyssey in high school, and Christopher Nolan didn't disappoint."

Top 3 picks for the ultimate beach read?
"I'm currently enjoying Yesteryear, like most people this summer. Earlier this summer I read Purple State, a fun slow-burn summer read, and next up is Judge Stone, a legal thriller collab from James Patterson and Viola Davis."

On getting your pages in: "Like most things, starting small is always a good way to get some success under your belt. Set manageable goals, like reading three pages a day, and before you know it, it will become the part of your day that you cannot miss."

Comforting books and shows for when you need a break — Wellness Pix

Hi, friend!

When summer turns into heavy heat and hazy skies, the summertime sadness can creep in. If you’re feeling blue, lean into gentler company with the kind of cozy shows and warm conversations that let you relax. Today’s picks are here to help you feel a little more human while taking care of yourself. Let’s get into it.

Author Spotlight

Oliver Burkeman is a British journalist and author known for challenging productivity, time management, and self-improvement culture. His writing blends psychology, philosophy, and humor to help readers make peace with their limitations during trying times rather than constantly trying to push past them.

Four Thousand Weeks

When summer feels like an overwhelming marathon of events, Burkeman offers relief: you were never meant to do it all. Reach for this guide when the FOMO gets loud—it's a quiet, steadying reminder that missing a few pool days won't cost you the meaningful life you're after.

Meditations for Mortals

This national bestseller is built for the days when your motivation is low or you’re stuck inside. These bite-sized daily reflections meet you where you are, no big life overhaul required. Think of it as your “OK” to let today just be what it is.

Great Escapes Indoors

Enjoy wellness tips and entertainment in your home by putting on a docuseries that takes you to far-off places.

Live to 100: Secrets of the Blue Zones

Streaming on Netflix

Explorer Dan Buettner travels to the world's longest-living communities — from Sardinia to Okinawa — uncovering the diet, movement, and social habits behind their longevity, and distilling his findings into lessons anyone can apply.

Down to Earth with Zac Efron

Streaming on Netflix

Zac Efron circles the globe with wellness expert Darin Olien, exploring sustainable food systems, clean energy, and healthy living in places like Iceland, Peru, and Sardinia. Together, they prove eco-conscious living can be both impactful and genuinely fun.

Podcasts to Keep You Company

Some days you just need a voice in your ear that gets it.

Ten Percent Happier

Hosted by journalist and bestselling author Dan Harris, this podcast features candid conversations with meditation teachers, scientists, and public figures on mindfulness, mental health, and finding calm — all with humor and zero new-age pretension for the reluctant self-improver.

Unlocking Us

Brené Brown hosts intimate, research-grounded conversations about vulnerability, courage, and connection with guests ranging from authors to athletes. Each episode digs into what it means to be human, offering comfort and insight for anyone navigating hard emotions.

I also learned many people are surprisingly determined to eat popcorn and drink soda at 6 a.m., but that's neither here nor there.

Romance | Out 8/11

3 Irish picks you’re missing out on

Welcome back to Insider Pix, where we uncover what entertainment and culture insiders are watching, reading, and listening to! Next up:

Dermot McCormack

Dermot McCormack is a transformational CEO, President, and investor with a track record of scaling media, streaming, and technology companies through bold strategy, operational excellence, and creative disruption. Today, he is CEO and Founder of Bravo Mondo, a growth-stage advisory and investment firm.

Dermot’s 5 Picks

A 5-star-worthy book you’d recommend to anyone?

The Undoing Project by Michael Lewis

Best movie you watched recently?

Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die (now streaming on Hulu)

Best TV show you’ve watched recently?

The Dry from RTE & ITV

A hidden gem you wish more people knew about?

Probably not a hidden gem but Desert Island Discs from the BBC. They put all episodes for over 30 years or more up as a podcast. It’s basically your favorite songs and a book and one item you would bring to a desert island.

Go-to weekly podcast?

Raging Moderates with Scott Gallaoway & Jessica Tarlov

Pix: Having been born and raised in Dublin, what are your top 3 picks of Irish media that you think every American should check out?

DM: Music: Glen Hansard

Movie: In Bruges, starring Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson

TV show: The Dry

Pix: What's one piece of entertainment—whether it's a documentary, podcast, or book—that you think every entrepreneur should experience, and why?

DM: If you are an entrepreneur or starting a company of any type, please read Shoe Dog by Phil Knight about the story of Nike…and then don’t do it!! Just kidding.

Pix: You've spent your career at the intersection of media and technology. What's one entertainment trend you're genuinely excited about right now?

DM: I’m working on several projects that blend the physical and digital in terms of narrative. Think immersive or experiential (although we need better words). Because a whole generation has been doing less and less in the physical world, I think entertainment will step in and fill some of this gap but be blended with new digital experiences. Think the Sphere, Cosm, or Outernet in London! This is a really exiting and fun trend in my view.

Pix: Looking back at your MTV and digital media days, what was the first moment that made you realize the way people consumed entertainment was fundamentally changing? How have those experiences shaped the way you think about AI in entertainment today?

DM: I think when Lost was the first show that came out and you could buy episodes from iTunes for your Mac and iPod! It was the first show I watched solely in a non-traditional TV environment. It also just happens to be an awesome show. I would watch on planes!

What it tells me about AI in entertainment today is, first of all, the entertainment had to be great. No amount of technology will make a bad story into a great story (yet). In the Lost example, technology gave the audience more choice for content and flexibility on how, when, and where you could watch. Hopefully, AI will allow new stories from new voices in ways we could never imagine and will democratize who gets to make what. There will also be some bad effects that I assume, if you are reading this, you can imagine. The Gold Standard for Superhero TV

Superhero fans have been spoiled with countless new shows over the last decade. But still nothing comes close to this 34-year-old masterpiece.

Batman: The Animated Series

By day, Bruce Wayne is a Gotham City billionaire. By night, he's Batman, patrolling a city crawling with costumed criminals who are just as damaged as he is. With Season 2 of Batman: Caped Crusader premiering on Friday, now's the perfect time for a rewatch!

Before Tom Holland ever put on the suit, one movie made Peter Parker a household name, and it still holds up over twenty years later.

Spider-Man

A shy teenager gets bitten by a genetically modified spider and quickly learns that with great power comes great responsibility. Tobey Maguire's Peter Parker stars opposite Willem Dafoe's Green Goblin in Sam Raimi's 2002 classic. Good Eats with Alton Brown. It was integral to my childhood/adolescence because it taught me not only how to cook, but why certain cooking methods worked. Food TV used to trust viewers to be curious; now, so much of it has been gamified and cartoonified into something I find incredibly boring. Alton Brown made people care enough about their food to want to understand it, cook it well, and enjoy it properly. I miss shows like that.

Best TV show you've watched recently?

Anne Rice's The Vampire Lestat (season three of Interview with the Vampire). It's trashy, wildly campy, and the acting is far better than anything this gloriously over the top show has a right to be.

Best movie you watched recently?

The Devil's Rain. Ernest Borgnine is a perfect little satanic freak in it, the cast is bizarrely stacked, and the whole movie is exactly the kind of strange, gooey 1970s horror I love.

A 5-star-worthy book you'd recommend to anyone?

A Prayer for Owen Meany by John Irving. At its center is a lifelong friendship between the narrator and Owen, a tiny boy with a permanently damaged voice who believes he knows exactly how and when he'll die. It's a funny, infuriating, heartbreaking novel about faith, fate, and the people who permanently rearrange your life. I find myself returning to it every few years, and I get something new out of it with each revisit.

Go-to weekly podcast?

Woo Woo with Rachel Dratch. It hits the perfect sweet spot between paranormal storytelling and comedy, with celebrity guests sharing their strangest encounters. As a host, Rachel is curious without being credulous and skeptical without ruining the fun, which is exactly how I like my woo-woo.

Pix: What cookbook has earned a permanent spot on your shelf?

MS: It's a tie between Every Day Is Saturday by Sarah Copeland and The Food Lab by J. Kenji López-Alt. Copeland's recipes are incredibly accessible but still beautiful and impressive, whether you're feeding a crowd or just your family on a random Tuesday. Nothing is particularly flashy or mind-blowing, which is exactly what I like about it. The Food Lab feeds my endless curiosity about the hows and whys of cooking, much like Good Eats did when I was growing up.

Pix: If logistics were no obstacle, what dishes are you including in your hypothetical final meal?

MS: I want chicken Francese from literally anywhere because I've never had a bad version, New England clam chowder from the dearly departed Cappy's Chowder House in Camden, ME, a Cali carnitas burrito from And Breakfast Burritos in San Diego, and ribs from Jack's Bar-B-Que in Nashville. I'd also need my mom's pot roast with red cabbage, schnitzel from Mountain Brauhaus in Gardiner, NY, banoffee ice cream from Fortunes in Tivoli, NY, and whatever is being served at the monthly Persian feast at Brushland Eating House in Bovina, NY—my favorite restaurant in the entire world.

Pix: Is there a restaurant dish you've had this year that you can't stop thinking about?

MS: The biscuits and gravy at Jax Diner in Portsmouth, RI. I stopped there on the way home from a wedding in Providence after plans to visit a nearby IHOP fell through, which now feels like divine intervention. The place is tiny, the menu is exactly as expansive as a diner menu should be, and everything is made in-house. I would love nothing more than to drown myself in their perfectly peppered sausage gravy.

Your next book binge obsession is missing pants

For weeks now, I've been afflicted with something that's completely derailed my productivity and kept me up at all hours. Don't worry, it's not the parasite that's forcing us all to abstain from berries and bagged salad. It's Dungeon Crawler Carl-itis. I can’t stop reading and talking about this bizarre sci-fi series. And I’m far from alone. (Seth MacFarlane is even turning it into a show.)

Reader, I'm officially converted. I never thought this series would be for me. On paper, Dungeon Crawler Carl (DCC) sounds like the exact kind of book I'd, um, politely admire from afar. But it won me over anyway, and I think that's the secret to its success: it's not just for gamers or sci-fi/fantasy fans. It's for anyone who needs a laugh, anyone who's found themselves rooting for an underdog during the World Cup, and anyone who could really use a win right now.

An aging nobleman reads too many romantic tales of chivalry, becomes convinced he's a knight, and recruits a farmer, Sancho Panza, as his squire. Written by Miguel de Cervantes in 1605, it's widely considered the first modern novel and still the most influential book to come out of Spain.

5 picks from our podcast expert — Insider Pix

Hi, friend!

Welcome back to Insider Pix, where we uncover what entertainment and culture insiders are watching, reading, and listening to! Next up:

Steve Raizes

Steve Raizes has spent 15 years in audio, working on shows like 48 Hours, The Daily Show, and RuPaul's Drag Race. He covers podcasts for Pix Media, where he writes Worth the Listen. When he's not listening to podcasts, he's raising a 6-year-old and a ragdoll cat (possibly not in that order).

Steve’s 5 Picks

Your go-to weekly podcast?

All the stuff from Puck and Ankler. Fun, smart, not afraid to poke at the sacred cows (less fun when you are a sacred cow).

A 5-star-worthy book you’d recommend to anyone?

Podcasters don’t read books.

I kid. What is a book again? Really enjoyed Long Island Compromise. Fun, smart, really great prose and a narrative that continued to twist and turn in interesting directions.

Best TV show you’ve watched recently?

I got pulled into Summer House. Was it the “best” TV show I have watched? Probably not. Was it deeply compelling? Yes, yes it was. I also watched Big Mistakes, which I thought was great. Maybe we do that one. Let’s do that one. Don’t tell anyone about Summer House. Why are you still typing?

Best movie you saw in theaters recently?

Saw Toy Story 5 with my kid and it blew his little mind. Strongly recommend (although now I’m having a lot of residual guilt over the amount of iPad the kid is getting, so…will need to reconcile that at some point in the future).

Unexpected side complication: Now having extended discussions about which of his toys should be able to talk and whether we, as a family, need to start better encouraging them to speak up.

A hidden gem you wish more people knew about?

Worth the Listen by Steve Raizes. That guy is super talented.

OR

No, no, I think it’s still Worth the Listen by Steve Raizes.

Pix: We’ll get our most controversial question out of the way first: What speed do you listen to podcasts at?

SR: 2x for all non-narrative pods—so anything that is purely informational in nature. For things that are story-driven, I definitely want it at 1x. If I am asked about this directly ever again, I will lie and say I listen only at 1x, as god intended, and that anything else is sacrilege.

(But once you get used to 2x, it is amazing how much you can consume, and it really doesn’t feel fast at all.)

Pix: You revealed in Worth the Listen your love for reality TV (and even a brief stint as a reality star). If you had to choose, which reality show would you join today?

SR: My greatest sadness in reality TV life is that I have never been able to play on Survivor. For a while, I was employed by Paramount, which fully prohibited me from playing on Survivor. Now I think I can play. However, now I would be the guy on Survivor playing with grey hair and reconciling his youth on national TV, so that’s a bit of a wrinkle I need to consider.
